channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: The Theft of an Old Mate
item.description: Keith Dunstan's Malvern Star bicycle is stolen during Bicycle Week in Swanston Street, prompting reflections on the irreplaceable intimacy of a well-worn saddle, a cross-country American saddle swap on a 1976 ride through Kansas, and the indignity of the $75 Kryptonite lock that was needed to protect the replacement.

item.title: The Achilles Knee
item.description: A survey of the epidemic of knee injuries in Australian football, with the argument that Polly Farmer's knee was the biggest news story of 1962, that the cartilage is God's most poorly designed joint, and that there should be a Cartilage Council alongside the Heart Foundation and Anti-Cancer Council.

item.title: Champagne is for Inside Not Outside
item.description: A proposal for a Society for the Restoration of Dignity in Sport, arguing that champagne hosing (which began with Australian cricketers) should be banned, that fieldsmen who take catches should remain unkissed, and that winning batsmen should shake hands rather than run headlong into each other's arms.

item.title: Our Muscular Christianity Beats Everything
item.description: A proposed Fourth Law of Motion applied to Australian sport coverage, arguing that the greater the victory the greater the hometown press, that Australia being thrashed in Pakistan barely rated a headline, and that losing gracefully abroad might actually generate more publicity than winning.

item.title: Why Not Retrospective Wilkies?
item.description: The VFL's decision to hand out retroactive Brownlow Medals to players who tied in the past prompts a suggestion that the same principle be applied to all Australian life, with a full list of those who should receive belated honours, concluding with shifting Bob Hawke to the House of Lords.

item.title: Spare Us the Arsehole
item.description: Derryn Hinch's on-air farewell shot at 3AW prompts a history of forbidden language in Australian newspapers, from the 1940s taboo on bodily functions through the gradual admission of 'damn' in 1962, 'bloody' in 1968, and the momentous newspaper debut of the word that finally gives this chapter its title.

item.title: The Crafty Creature's Guide to Sex
item.description: A practical guide for identifying male from female in the age of Boy George and androgyny, covering jeans, tops, sneakers, smoking, hair, ear rings, newspapers, posture, and make-up, with the author confessing he once managed to overtake a female jogger only because she had stopped to do up a shoelace.

item.title: Please Can We Continue to Have Sex?
item.description: A defence of sex in advertising and art against the Commonwealth Style Manual's drive to eliminate gendered language and a minister's campaign against female exploitation, citing Michelangelo, Norman Lindsay and Rubens, and arguing that the joy of ice cream ads and soft drink commercials is all we have left.

item.title: How to Love Female Muscle
item.description: A confession that Martina Navratilova's forehand photograph, her biceps brachii and her gastrocnemius are a source of inspiration, with reflections on the new breed of muscular female jogger who leaves the author at the speed of a space shuttle, and a rebuke for Hana Mandlikova's unkind remarks about Martina at Wimbledon.

item.title: Melbourne's Most Virginal Bosom
item.description: An exclusive interview with Chloe at Young & Jackson's Hotel on the proposed illuminated sign of her outline, her 1883 arrival from Paris, the chorus of protests at the National Gallery's International Exhibition, the American serviceman who threw a glass of beer at her in 1943, and her frank preference for the men's bar over avocado salads.

item.title: Your Intimate Guide to the Dangers of Marriage
item.description: A Monash University survey finding 80 per cent of families fight over breakfast prompts a rival independent survey introducing the Marital Stress Factor scale, rating garden disagreements at MSF68, picture framing at MSF65, watching football at MSF80, going out to parties at MSF72 and keeping the house in show condition for five minutes before guests arrive as the most awesome moment of all.

item.title: Adjusting the Set after Grandchildren
item.description: Eleven grandchildren depart after the Easter holidays leaving a house full of mementos, a boomerang on the roof, a baby's dummy by the telephone, digital clocks set to strange hours, an Alice in Wonderland video locked on child lock, and a four-year-old's parting observation that the author hasn't got much fur.

item.title: Auctions Are Close to Rape and Murder
item.description: The end of football season triggers the auction season, and keeping a house in show condition for six weeks — with strangers going through rear cupboards three times a week — turns out to be a crash course in real estate agent language, in which 'retention dreams' means don't lean against the weatherboards, and 'delightful bush setting' means a colony of possums.

item.title: What Hands Did They Have on the Titanic?
item.description: A confession that the household is into bridge, covering Auto Bridge machines, home computer opponents, the perils of playing with one's wife, the deaf-mute partner at duplicate, the kidnapping of Edith Rosenkrantz at the North American championships, and the bridge players on the Titanic who kept playing because they didn't know it had sprung a leak.

item.title: Don't Dare Knock Clocks
item.description: Paul Keating's public admission of his passion for antique clocks prompts a defence of the collector, a distinction between soulless digital clocks and the honest mechanical tick, an account of the wife's 'no more than two clocks per room' rule, and the joy of hearing them chime three, four, five o'clock in the night.

item.title: Could I Be a Token Male?
item.description: Prompted by the news that female committee membership is now compulsory, a look at Edmund Cooper's novel in which by 2043 the ratio of females to males is twelve to five and men are needed only for stud purposes, with a plea that when the position is reversed the powerful female prime ministers will appoint a token male to a board here and there.

item.title: The Bliss of Owning a Pool
item.description: A possessions-scoring game that rates swimming pools at a pitiful 3 points frames the story of the fibreglass pool that came with the house in 1977, the pool man who ran his stethoscope over the pump and found $520 worth of problems, and a friend at Mooroolbark who gave his pool away in a truck and planted a jacaranda, feeling liberated.

item.title: Don't Hang Up on Phone Callers
item.description: Telephone addiction is ranked among the most serious drugs, ahead of alcohol and tobacco, with evidence including a mother whose bill from Minnesota reached $400, the futility of 'Maximum three minutes' notices above the telephone, the exotic new handsets Telecom produces as inviting as lollipops, and a suggestion that whoever makes local calls free will be Prime Minister for a generation.

item.title: Foreword
item.description: Barry Humphries' foreword to 'Knockers', a mock-defensive survey of Australian knockery aimed at expatriates, critics and the film industry, recalling his own drubbing over an 'Aussie slang shocks Britain' headline and Dick Bentley's BBC Australia Day broadcast.

item.title: Knockers
item.description: Opens 'Knockers' by tracing the Australian compulsion to cut down its own achievers, from a Melbourne newspaper importing a London editor to soothe its colonial cringe, through visiting critics from James Cameron to Clement Freud, to the vicious reception of the Sydney Opera House and Australian writers at home.

item.title: Introduction
item.description: Opens 'No Brains on Tuesday' by recounting Keith Dunstan's 1985 defection from the Sun News-Pictorial, where his father had been General Manager, to write for the Age and Sydney Morning Herald, and the guilt, gracious phone calls and one cold shoulder that followed.

item.title: Who Smashes the Beethoven, Bach and Brahms LPs?
item.description: A column on the death of the vinyl LP as Polygram stops pressing new titles, tracing Keith Dunstan's own audio history from an HMV portable gramophone and 78s smashed with a hammer through to CD and the first Compact Disc Video players.

item.title: Your De-palatisation Guide
item.description: A tongue-in-cheek training program for wine lovers priced out of Grange Hermitage and Veuve Cliquot, working down through the grades to Coolibah cask at $7.99, extended to equivalent deprogramming courses for golfers, Bridge addicts, chocolate lovers and the incurable football fan.

item.title: There's Sex in Lolly Water
item.description: A survey of increasingly sexualised soft drink advertising, from Coca-Cola's frenzy and Tina Turner's writhing for Pepsi to spa water ads that promise everything, contrasted against the strict codes preventing beer advertisers from suggesting any pleasurable effect at all, with three proposed scenarios showing how soft drink ads could instead honestly reflect Australian life.

item.title: Dear Viewer
item.description: Episode four of the winemaking mini-series, in which toy poodle Lotte defeats the starlings, three tonnes of pinot noir are harvested, a power crusher replaces the virgins, and an electric blanket and hair dryer are requisitioned from the house for malolactic fermentation.

item.title: Loving Messages from the Chairman
item.description: An appreciative survey of the increasingly lavish company annual reports arriving in the letterbox, from the National Australia Bank's directors wandering elegantly down a marble staircase to the Lend Lease report's sapphire-blue portrait of Mr Dusseldorp and a ballerina held aloft by a site carpenter.

item.title: Would a Tax on the Waistline Help?
item.description: A detailed proposal for NICK, the New Inspired Consumption Kill, as a more rational alternative to the consumption tax, targeting automobiles for their emissions, graffiti pens, plastic bags, outdoor advertising, noisy motorbikes, television repeats, corporate take-over bids and the booming diet industry.

item.title: The Intelligent Man's Budget Guide
item.description: An A-to-Z economic dictionary for the bewildered citizen, defining Accord, Deficit, Gearing, J-curve, Pipeline and Zero in terms of actual Australian experience under Hawke, Keating and Kirner rather than Treasury optimism.

item.title: A Prostate Could Make You AA
item.description: The indignities of the modern credit-rating system, from Moody's down-grading the State Bank and a credit card application requiring a month-long inquisition, to an automatic teller swallowing a card and a South Yarra liquor store refusing a cheque, culminating in the observation that Bob Hawke's prostate operation will surely restore his public approval rating to Aaa.

item.title: Do Any of us Get Paid Enough?
item.description: A column on fair wages, arguing that a Flinders baker, Montsalvat violin and piano makers, leg spin bowlers, teachers, priests and policemen are chronically underpaid while golfers, share brokers, disc jockeys and newspaper columnists are a more interesting question altogether.
